### WHAT IT IS
The **Computer Training Centres (Regulation) Bill, 2004** was introduced by Shri Iqbal Ahmed Saradgi, M.P., to regulate computer training centres in India, mandate compulsory registration, prescribe syllabi and fee structures, and curb exploitative practices such as abrupt closures and exorbitant fees [1, 2, 3].

### OWNERSHIP & LEGAL STATUS
- **Proponent / Ministry**: Private Member Bill introduced by Shri Iqbal Ahmed Saradgi, M.P. [1]. Implementation and enforcement are assigned to the **appropriate Government** (Central Government or State Government, as the case may be) [1, 4].
- **Legal Status**: Introduced legislation (not an Act in force) [1].

### PENALTIES UNDER THE BILL
Under **Clause 10** of the Computer Training Centres (Regulation) Bill, 2004, any person who violates the provisions of the proposed Act faces the following mandatory minimum penalties [5]:

| Penalty Type | Minimum Statutory Requirement |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Imprisonment** | Term **not less than three years** [5] |
| **Fine** | **Not less than ₹1,00,000** (one lakh rupees) [5] |

### TRADE-OFFS & IMPLEMENTATION WATCH
- **Case for**: Protects students from unaccredited institutes charging excessive fees and shutting down without finishing coursework [3].
- **Case against / Gaps**: Imposes severe minimum custodial sentences (minimum 3 years) and high minimum monetary penalties without judicial discretion to scale down sentences based on minor compliance infractions [5].

### WHAT IT IS
The **Computer Training Centres (Regulation) Bill, 2004** was introduced in the Lok Sabha by Shri Iqbal Ahmed Saradgi, M.P., to regulate private computer training centres, mandate compulsory registration, and curb unfair practices such as charging exorbitant fees or shutting down operations mid-course after taking tuition fees from students [1, 2].

### PENAL PROVISIONS (TERM OF IMPRISONMENT & FINE)
Under **Clause 10** of the Computer Training Centres (Regulation) Bill, 2004, any person who violates the provisions of the Act is liable to:

* **Minimum term of imprisonment:** **Not less than three years** [3].
* **Minimum fine:** **Not less than ₹1,00,000 (one lakh rupees)** [3].

### DESIGN & REGULATORY MECHANISM
* **Compulsory Registration:** Clause 3 bars any person from running a computer centre without prior registration with the appropriate Government [4]. Existing and newly proposed centres must apply within one month from commencement [5].
* **Standards & Fee Fixation:** The appropriate Government is empowered to scrutinise applications, verify prerequisites, and prescribe the syllabus and fees for each course [6, 7].
* **Enforcement & Cancellation:** Upon receiving a complaint, the appropriate Government must investigate and decide within one month; if substantiated, registration must be cancelled forthwith [8].

### **WHAT IT IS**
The Computer Training Centres (Regulation) Bill, 2004 is a private member's legislative proposal introduced in the Lok Sabha by Shri Iqbal Ahmed Saradgi, M.P., to regulate private computer training institutions, mandate their prior registration, standardize syllabi and fees, and protect students from unaccredited centres charging exorbitant fees or closing operations mid-course [1, 2, 3].

### **OWNERSHIP & LEGAL STATUS**
* **Sponsor / Ownership:** Private Member's Bill introduced by **Shri Iqbal Ahmed Saradgi, M.P.** [2].
* **Statutory vs Executive:** Proposed primary legislation (Private Member's Bill) [2].
* **Chamber & Date:** Introduced in the Lok Sabha; dated **18 August 2004** [2, 4].

### **DESIGN**
* **Registration Requirement:** Section 3 prohibits any person from running a computer centre without prior registration with the appropriate Government [5]. Existing and new centres must apply for registration within **one month** of the Act's commencement under Section 4 [5].
* **Curriculum & Fee Regulation:** Section 7 empowers the appropriate Government to prescribe syllabus and fees for each course imparted by a computer centre [3].
* **Complaint & Deregistration Mechanism:** Under Section 8 and Section 9, complaints regarding a centre must be investigated and decided within **one month**, and upon finding the complaint in order, registration is cancelled forthwith [3].
* **Penalties (Section 10):**
  * **Minimum term of imprisonment:** **Not less than three years** [1].
  * **Minimum fine:** **Not less than ₹1,00,000 (one lakh rupees)** [1].

### **TRADE-OFFS**
* **In Support (from the Record):** Halts the proliferation of unaccredited centres operating without basic facilities or standard course contents, curbing sudden closures after charging steep upfront student fees [6].
* **In Concern (Inference from Record Design):** Imposes severe minimum custodial penalties (minimum 3 years' imprisonment) and fixed minimum fines with no statutory ceiling or judicial discretion specified in the clause text, creating heavy regulatory compliance risks for private training operators [1].

### WHAT IT IS
Under **The Copyright (Second Amendment) Bill, 1992**, the proposed provision to permit the adaptation of software for debugging purposes was the insertion of a new **clause (aa)** into sub-section (1) of **section 52** of the Copyright Act, 1957 [1] [2]. This amendment sought to exempt from copyright infringement the making of copies or adaptations by the lawful possessor of a computer programme in order to utilise the programme for its intended purpose (which the Notes on Clauses specifically identifies as covering legitimate debugging requirements) [1] [2].

### OWNERSHIP & LEGAL STATUS
* **Ministry / In-charge:** Ministry of Human Resource Development (introduced by Shri Arjun Singh) [3] [4].
* **Status / Stage:** Bill as introduced in the Lok Sabha (Bill No. 106 of 1992, introduced on **6 July 1992**) [4].
* **Nature:** Legislative amendment proposal amending the Copyright Act, 1957 [4].

### DESIGN OF THE PROVISION
According to the text of the Bill and its Notes on Clauses:

1. **Proposed Section 52(1)(aa):** Clause 17(3) of the Bill sought to insert clause `(aa)` into Section 52(1), providing that the following acts would not constitute an infringement of copyright [2]:
   > *"(aa) the making of copies of adaptation of a computer programme by the lawful possessor of a copy of such computer programme, from such copy—*
   > *(i) in order to utilise the computer programme for the purpose for which it was supplied; or*
   > *(ii) to make back-up copies purely as a temporary protection against loss, destruction or damage in order only to utilise the computer programme for the purpose for which it was supplied;"* [2]

2. **Purpose Identified in Notes on Clauses:** The Notes on Clauses for Clause 17 clarified that this insertion was specifically intended *"to cover the legitimate requirement of the lawful owner of a copy of a computer programme to make adaptations for 'debugging' and to make back-up copies"* [1].

3. **Moral Rights Safeguard (Proviso to Section 57):** In parallel, Clause 20 sought to amend **section 57** (author’s special rights) by inserting a proviso stating that the author shall not have any right to restrain or claim damages in respect of any adaptation of a computer programme to which clause (aa) of sub-section (1) of section 52 applies, specifically safeguarding lawful debugging adaptations from claims of author's moral rights infringement [5] [6].

### TRADE-OFFS
* **Case For:** Recognised that legitimate, bona fide users and lawful possessors require the flexibility to fix errors ("debug") and create backup copies so the software functions for the purpose it was supplied, without facing civil infringement or criminal penalties [1] [2].
* **Case Against / Safeguards:** To curb software piracy, general private study reproduction rights for computer programmes under Section 52(1)(a) were simultaneously restricted, and Section 63C was introduced to make knowing use of infringing computer programmes a punishable offence [1] [7].

### IMPLEMENTATION WATCH
* **Subsequent Revisions:** The proposal in the 1992 Bill laid the groundwork for provisions later enacted through the **Copyright (Amendment) Act, 1994** (which codified Section 52(1)(aa)) and subsequent refinements in the **Copyright (Amendment) Bill, 1999** regarding reverse engineering and interoperability [8].

### WHAT IT IS
Under the **Copyright (Second Amendment) Bill, 1992**, the adaptation of software for debugging purposes was provided for by inserting a statutory fair-dealing exemption into **Section 52(1)** of the Copyright Act, 1957, alongside a corresponding limitation on the author's special moral rights under **Section 57** [2, 3, 8, 17].

### OWNERSHIP & LEGAL STATUS
* **Ministry:** Ministry of Human Resource Development (introduced by Arjun Singh, Minister of Human Resource Development) [33].
* **Instrument:** Legislative Bill amending the Copyright Act, 1957 (Bill introduced in the Lok Sabha) [5, 33].
* **Date:** Introduced in 1992 (Notice/Bill text dated 6 May 1992 / 6 July 1992) [30, 33].

### DESIGN
To permit adaptation for "debugging" and legitimate operation without constituting copyright infringement, the Bill proposed the following specific provisions:

1. **Insertion of Section 52(1)(aa):**
   Clause 17(3) of the Bill proposed inserting clause `(aa)` in sub-section (1) of Section 52 to make non-infringing [3, 8]:
   > *"(aa) the making of copies of adaptation of a computer programme by the lawful possessor of a copy of such computer programme, from such copy—*
   > *(i) in order to utilise the computer programme for the purpose for which it was supplied; or*
   > *(ii) to make back-up copies purely as a temporary protection against loss, destruction or damage in order only to utilise the computer programme for the purpose for which it was supplied;"* [8]
   
   *Note on Notes on Clauses:* The Notes on Clauses specifically recorded that the new clause `(aa)` was inserted to *"cover the legitimate requirement of the lawful owner of a copy of a computer programme to make adaptations for 'debugging' and to make back-up copies"* [3, 7].

2. **Consequential Proviso to Section 57(1) (Moral Rights):**
   To ensure authors could not use moral rights against lawful debugging adaptations, Clause 20 inserted a proviso to Section 57(1) [2, 17]:
   > *"Provided that the author shall not have any right to restrain or claim damages in respect of any adaptation of a computer programme to which clause (aa) of sub-section (1) of section 52 applies."* [17]

3. **Exclusion from General Private Use:**
   Sub-clause (2) of Clause 17 concurrently amended Section 52(1)(a) to add the words *", not being computer programme,"* after *"artistic work"*, explicitly excluding computer programs from general private reproduction while carving out debugging and backup rights under the dedicated clause `(aa)` [3, 8].

### TRADE-OFFS
* **Case For:** Recognises the practical necessity of allowing legitimate users and lawful possessors to debug, adapt, and run software to achieve intended functionality without facing civil liability or criminal exposure [3, 8].
* **Case Against / Restrictive Boundary:** Confined strictly to the lawful possessor from their authorised copy to avoid creating broad, unmonitored private copying exemptions that could facilitate commercial software piracy [3, 13].

### IMPLEMENTATION WATCH
* Track the final enacted wording under the **Copyright (Amendment) Act, 1994** (Act 38 of 1994), where Section 52(1)(aa) was codified into law.
* Monitor subsequent expansions in the **Copyright (Amendment) Act, 1999**, which inserted Sections 52(1)(ab), (ac), and (ad) for interoperability, observation/testing of ideas, and non-commercial personal use [14].

### WHAT IT IS
Under **The Copyright (Second Amendment) Bill, 1992**, the adaptation of software for debugging purposes was provided for by exempting specific user actions from copyright infringement and carving out exceptions to authors' moral rights [2][3]. The Bill proposed inserting a new **clause (aa) into sub-section (1) of section 52** of the Copyright Act, 1957, alongside a corresponding proviso to **section 57(1)** [3][8][17].

### OWNERSHIP & LEGAL STATUS
* **Ministry / Sponsor:** Introduced by **Arjun Singh**, Minister of Human Resource Development, in the **Lok Sabha** on **6 July 1992** [33].
* **Instrument Type:** Statutory amendment bill (amending the Copyright Act, 1957) [5].
* **Status in Record:** As-introduced text / legislative proposal [5].

### DESIGN
The framework enabling adaptation and debugging consists of two core statutory provisions:

1. **Insertion of Section 52(1)(aa) (Acts Not Constituting Infringement):**
   Clause 17 of the Bill amends section 52(1) to insert clause `(aa)`, declaring that copyright is not infringed by:
   > *"the making of copies of adaptation of a computer programme by the lawful possessor of a copy of such computer programme, from such copy—*
   > *(i) in order to utilise the computer programme for the purpose for which it was supplied; or*
   > *(ii) to make back-up copies purely as a temporary protection against loss, destruction or damage in order only to utilise the computer programme for the purpose for which it was supplied;"* [8].
   
   The Notes on Clauses explain that this amendment was designed *"to cover the legitimate requirement of the lawful owner of a copy of a computer programme to make adaptations for 'debugging' and to make back-up copies"* while simultaneously excluding computer programmes from the general private-use exemption under section 52(1)(a) [3][7].

2. **Limitation on Author's Moral Rights (Section 57):**
   To ensure authors could not block debugging modifications under the banner of distortion or modification prejudicial to honour or reputation, Clause 20 amends section 57(1) to add a specific proviso:
   > *"Provided that the author shall not have any right to restrain or claim damages in respect of any adaptation of a computer programme to which clause (aa) of sub-section (1) of section 52 applies."* [2][17].

### TRADE-OFFS
* **In Support:** Protects bona fide end-users and lawful owners by legalising necessary modifications, bug fixes, operational adaptations, and temporary archival/back-up copies essential for software functionality [3][8].
* **In Caution / Restrictions:** Excludes computer programmes from general *"private use"* reproduction exceptions under section 52(1)(a) to protect software developers from unwarranted unlicensed copying [3][8], and penalises knowing use of infringing software copies under proposed section 63C [13][21].

### IMPLEMENTATION WATCH
* **Enactment & Notification Tracking:** Track whether these clauses were incorporated into the final Copyright (Amendment) Act, 1994 or subsequent amending Acts [4][5].
* **Judicial Scope of "Lawful Possessor":** Track regulatory interpretations regarding the boundary between permissible debugging/interoperability and unauthorised commercial modification or reverse engineering [8][14].

### WHAT IT IS
Under **Clause 3** of **The Special Educational Facilities for Children of Manual Scavengers Bill, 2001** (Bill No. LXX of 2001), the appropriate government is mandated to identify eligible beneficiaries by conducting field surveys and maintaining formal beneficiary registers within its territorial jurisdiction [1][2].

### OWNERSHIP & LEGAL STATUS
* **Instrument:** Private Member's Bill introduced in the Rajya Sabha by Shri S. S. Ahluwalia, M.P. [1][3].
* **Enacted Status:** Introduced bill (not enacted into law) [1].
* **Appropriate Government Defined:** Defined under **Clause 2(a)** as the State Government in the case of a State, and the Central Government in other cases [1].

### DESIGN: BENEFICIARY IDENTIFICATION RESPONSIBILITIES
Under **Clause 3** ("Survey to be conducted by appropriate Government"), the specific statutory duties assigned to the appropriate government are:
1. **Conduct of Survey:** It is the duty of the appropriate government to conduct surveys in the area under its jurisdiction to find out the children of scavengers who are to be imparted education by such government [2].
2. **Preparation of Beneficiary Lists:** Prepare a list of such eligible children in such manner as may be prescribed [2].
3. **Periodic Revision:** Cause the prepared list to be revised at such intervals as may be prescribed [2].

### TRADE-OFFS & FINANCIAL IMPLICATIONS
* **Administrative Burden:** Entrusts comprehensive door-to-door or territorial enumeration to State and Central authorities to identify children of persons who were engaged or employed for manually carrying human excreta before the commencement of the 1993 Act [1][2].
* **Financial Requirements:** According to the Financial Memorandum, conducting the survey under Clause 3, providing educational facilities under Clause 4, and appointing Attendance Authorities under Clause 7 was estimated to require an annual recurring expenditure of approximately **₹100 crore** and a non-recurring expenditure of **₹10 crore** from the Consolidated Fund of India [4].

### IMPLEMENTATION WATCH
* **Rules Specification:** The exact procedures for conducting surveys, the listing formats, and revision frequencies were delegated to rules framed by the Central Government under **Clause 9** [2][5].
* **Enforcement Machinery:** Identification lists were intended to link directly to the Attendance Authorities empowered under **Clause 7** to monitor enrollment and attendance [5].

### WHAT IT IS
The **Special Educational Facilities for Children of Manual Scavengers Bill, 2001** (Private Member Bill No. LXX of 2001, introduced in the Rajya Sabha by Shri S.S. Ahluwalia) seeks to provide free education, hostel facilities, books, uniforms, transportation, and scholarships to children of scavengers or Safai Karamcharis who were engaged in or employed for manually carrying human excreta [1] [2] [3].

### IDENTIFICATION RESPONSIBILITY OF THE APPROPRIATE GOVERNMENT
Under **Clause 3** of the Bill, the responsibility for identifying eligible beneficiaries is explicitly mandated as follows:

* **Conduct of Survey:** It is the duty of the **appropriate Government** (defined under Clause 2(a) as the State Government in the case of a State, and the Central Government in other cases) to conduct a survey within the area under its jurisdiction to find out the children of scavengers [1] [4].
* **Preparation of Beneficiary List:** The appropriate Government must prepare a list, in such manner as may be prescribed, of such children who are to be imparted education by that government [4].
* **Periodic Revision:** The appropriate Government is required to cause this list to be revised at such intervals as may be prescribed [4].

### STATUTORY CONTEXT & BENEFICIARY CRITERIA
* **Scavenger Definition:** Clause 2(e) defines a "scavenger" as a person who had been engaged or employed for manually carrying human excreta prior to the commencement of the Employment of Manual Scavengers and Construction of Dry Latrines (Prohibition) Act, 1993 [5].
* **Enforcement Apparatus:** Under Clause 7, the appropriate Government is also empowered to appoint **Attendance Authorities** (and assisting personnel) to oversee implementation and ensure eligible children attend educational institutions [6].

### 1. WHAT IT IS
The **Special Educational Facilities for Children of Manual Scavengers Bill, 2001** is a private member's legislative proposal introduced in the Rajya Sabha to mandate free educational facilities—ranging from school level to post-graduate, medical, and technical education—along with hostels, books, and scholarships for the children of scavengers or Safai Karamcharis who were previously engaged in manually carrying human excreta [1], [4].

### 2. OWNERSHIP & LEGAL STATUS
* **Chamber & Sponsor:** Introduced in the **Rajya Sabha** as Bill No. LXX of 2001 by **Shri S. S. Ahluwalia, M.P.** [1], [9].
* **Legal Status:** Bill as introduced; not enacted into law [1].
* **Appropriate Government Defined:** Defined under **Clause 2(a)** as the **State Government** in the case of a State, and the **Central Government** in other cases [1].

### 3. DESIGN: RESPONSIBILITY FOR IDENTIFYING ELIGIBLE BENEFICIARIES
Under **Clause 3** of the Bill, the responsibility for identifying eligible beneficiaries is established as an explicit duty of the appropriate government [3]:

* **Mandatory Survey:** It is the duty of the appropriate government to conduct a survey in the area under its jurisdiction to find out the children of scavengers who are to be imparted education [2], [3].
* **Preparation of List:** The appropriate government must prepare a list of such eligible children in such manner as may be prescribed [3].
* **Periodic Revision:** The appropriate government is required to cause the list to be revised at such intervals as may be prescribed [3].
* **Administrative Support:** Under **Clause 7**, the appropriate government is empowered to appoint **Attendance Authorities** and assisting staff to enforce educational attendance and monitor cases where children are unable to attend full-time institutions due to family economic distress [5], [6].

### 4. TRADE-OFFS
* **Case for the Instrument:** Breaks generational cycles of manual scavenging by securing fully state-funded schooling, higher education, hostels, and stipends for children living below the poverty line [4], [11], [14].
* **Case against the Instrument:** Imposes an estimated recurring expenditure of **₹100 crore** per annum and a non-recurring outlay of **₹10 crore** on the Consolidated Fund of India [2], alongside administrative burdens on States to continuously survey and update beneficiary registers without specific enforcement penalties for bureaucratic default [3], [9].

### 5. IMPLEMENTATION WATCH
* **Prescribed Rules:** Scrutiny of rules framed under **Clause 9** by the Central Government defining the survey format, identification criteria, and revision intervals [6], [9].
* **Attendance Authority Deployments:** Monitoring the notification and staffing of Attendance Authorities under **Clause 7** across jurisdictions [5].

### WHAT IT IS
The **Right to Work Bill, 2002** was a Private Member's Bill introduced in the Lok Sabha by Shri G. M. Banatwalla to provide every adult citizen a legal right to appropriate work or an unemployment allowance (not less than ₹200 per week) until work is provided [1, 2, 3]. To finance these payments and administrative expenses, the Bill mandates the establishment of the **Right to Work Fund** [4, 5].

### OWNERSHIP & LEGAL STATUS
* **Ministry / Desk Oversight:** Ministry of Labour (Central Government) [6].
* **Instrument Type:** Private Member's Legislative Bill (Lok Sabha) [1, 6].
* **Status / Stage:** Introduced in Lok Sabha; recommended by the President under Articles 117(1), 117(3), and 274(1) of the Constitution [6].

### SOURCES CREDITED TO THE RIGHT TO WORK FUND
Under **Section 9(3)** of the Bill, the following five sources of revenue are mandated to be credited to the Right to Work Fund [4, 5]:

| Clause | Source of Revenue |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Section 9(3)(a)** | All grants made by the Central Government under sub-section (2) of Section 9 [4, 5]. |
| **Section 9(3)(b)** | All voluntary donations made to the Fund (which qualify for income-tax rebates/deductions under Section 11) [2, 4, 5]. |
| **Section 9(3)(c)** | All contributions in respect of the Right to Work Insurance Policy under Section 10 [4, 5]. |
| **Section 9(3)(d)** | All sums collected under Section 12 (mandatory contributions from citizens who receive work or allowance under the Act, for a prescribed period immediately after securing any work/job) [4, 5, 7]. |
| **Section 9(3)(e)** | Any interest, dividend, or other return on any investment made out of any part of the Fund [5]. |

### TRADE-OFFS & FINANCIAL DESIGN
* **Proponents' View:** Reduces long-term fiscal strain on the Consolidated Fund of India by creating a self-replenishing model via post-employment clawback contributions, voluntary donations, and dedicated insurance mechanisms [2, 8].
* **Burden / Drawback:** Imposes mandatory salary deductions on newly employed workers who previously drew allowances or obtained work through the scheme (Section 12), alongside an estimated recurring central liability of ₹500 crore per annum [7, 8].

### IMPLEMENTATION WATCH
* **Rule-Making Requirements:** Prescribing the exact rate and duration of contributions under Section 12 [7, 9].
* **Insurance Framework:** Development of the operational contours of the Right to Work Insurance Policy under Section 10 [5, 9].

### **WHAT IT IS**
The **Right to Work Bill, 2002** (introduced in the Lok Sabha by Shri G.M. Banatwalla, M.P.) provides for a legal right to work and guarantees an unemployment allowance (not less than ₹200 per week) to registered unemployed citizens until appropriate work is provided [1, 2, 4]. To finance the payment of allowances and related administrative costs, Section 9(1) of the Bill mandates the Central Government to establish the **Right to Work Fund** [1, 3].

---

### **OWNERSHIP & LEGAL STATUS**
* **Sponsor / Ministry Touchpoint:** Private Member Bill introduced by Shri G.M. Banatwalla, M.P. [4]; recommendation of the President conveyed by the Minister of Labour [7].
* **Nature:** Proposed statutory enactment (Bill as introduced in Lok Sabha) [4].
* **Administration:** Held and administered by the Central Government [1, 4].

---

### **DESIGN: MANDATED REVENUE SOURCES (SECTION 9(3))**
Under **Section 9(3)** of the Bill, the following five sources of revenue are mandated to be credited to the **Right to Work Fund** [1, 3]:

| Clause | Mandated Source of Revenue |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Section 9(3)(a)** | All grants made by the Central Government under Section 9(2) [1, 3] |
| **Section 9(3)(b)** | All voluntary donations made to the Fund [1, 3] |
| **Section 9(3)(c)** | All contributions in respect of the Right to Work Insurance Policy under Section 10 [1, 3] |
| **Section 9(3)(d)** | All sums collected under Section 12 (mandatory contributions from citizens who secure work or jobs after receiving work or allowance under the Act) [1, 3, 21] |
| **Section 9(3)(e)** | Any interest, dividend, or other return on any investment made out of any part of the Fund [3] |

---

### **TRADE-OFFS & IMPLEMENTATION WATCH**
* **Self-Financing Pathway vs. Initial Burden:** The Financial Memorandum estimated an initial recurring requirement of roughly ₹500 crore per annum from the Consolidated Fund of India, designed to taper as voluntary tax-rebated donations, Right to Work Insurance proceeds, and post-employment worker contributions materialise [2, 33].
* **Prescribed Rates & Scope:** The specific period and contribution rates for citizens securing employment under Section 12, as well as the operational architecture of the Right to Work Insurance scheme under Section 10, were left to delegated legislation / rules framed by the Central Government [19, 21].

### WHAT IT IS
The **Right to Work Bill, 2002** is a Private Member's Bill introduced in the Lok Sabha by Shri G.M. Banatwalla to provide citizens with a legal right to appropriate work or an unemployment allowance (not less than ₹200 per week) until work is provided [1, 2, 4]. To finance the grant of these allowances, the Bill establishes a dedicated **Right to Work Fund** [1, 3].

### MANDATED REVENUE SOURCES FOR THE FUND
Under **Section 9(3)** of the Bill, the following sources are mandated to be credited to the Right to Work Fund [1, 3]:

| Source | Statutory Provision | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Government Grants** | Section 9(3)(a) read with Section 9(2) | All grants made by the Central Government from time to time as required for the purposes of the Act [1, 3]. |
| **Voluntary Donations** | Section 9(3)(b) | All voluntary donations made to the Fund (which qualify for tax rebates/deductions under Section 11) [1, 2, 3]. |
| **Insurance Contributions** | Section 9(3)(c) read with Section 10 | All contributions in respect of the Right to Work Insurance Policy [1, 3]. |
| **Beneficiary Contributions** | Section 9(3)(d) read with Section 12 | All sums collected under Section 12, under which every citizen who secures work or receives an allowance under the Act is required to contribute to the Fund at a prescribed rate for a prescribed period immediately upon securing work [1, 3, 21]. |
| **Returns on Investments** | Section 9(3)(e) | Any interest, dividend, or other return on investments made out of any part of the Fund [3]. |

* **Status / Stage:** Introduced Bill (not enacted into law) [4]. Presidential recommendation was obtained under Articles 117(1), 117(3), and 274(1) of the Constitution via Ministry of Labour communication dated 19 April 2002 [7].

### Statutory Qualifications and Requirements
To qualify for designation and authorisation by the Central Government, an entity must satisfy the following statutory criteria:

1. **Form of Entity:** Must be an organisation, company, firm, or body of individuals [1], [2].
2. **Substantive Expertise & Knowledge:** Must possess:
   - **Expertise in matters relating to security**, and
   - **Knowledge of ship and port operations** [1], [2].
3. **Government Authorisation:** Must be authorised by the Central Government by **notification in the Official Gazette** [1], [2].
4. **Statutory Scope/Purpose:** The authorisation is granted to carry out:
   - Assessment, or
   - Verification, or
   - Approval, or
   - Certification,
   as required by Part IXB of the Act or by the **International Code for the Security of Ships and Port Facilities (ISPS Code)** [2].

Additionally, under the proviso to **Section 344M(2)**, the Central Government may authorise any recognised security organisation to carry out security measures on its behalf, subject to such conditions as may be prescribed [25].

### WHAT IT IS
Under the statutory design for guaranteed rural employment, when wages are directly linked with the quantity of work (piece-rate basis), the schedule of rates fixed by the State Government must ensure that an unskilled labourer working for a standard duration earns a wage equal to the prescribed daily wage rate [1].

### OWNERSHIP & LEGAL STATUS
* **Authority:** State Government, in consultation with the State Employment Guarantee Council [1].
* **Statutory Instrument:** National Rural Employment Guarantee legislation (Schedule I) [1], [2].
* **Conditionality:** Under no circumstances shall workers be paid less than the statutory wage rate [1].

### DESIGN

### 3. DESIGN
* **Primary Objective**: To fulfill the long-standing demand and political aspirations of the public of Delhi to have an effective voice in running their own administration by elevating Delhi from a Union Territory to a constituent State of the Union [77]. This followed the recommendations of a Committee appointed on **24 December 1987**, which submitted its report on **14 December 1989** [77].
* **Core Clauses & Structural Mechanisms**:
  * **Clause 1**: Title and commencement notification [24].
  * **Clause 2 (Insertion of Article 371J)**: Inserts new **Article 371J** after Article 371-I to govern the Capital State of Delhi [24]:
    * **Legislative Exclusion**: The Legislative Assembly of the Capital State of Delhi was expressly denied legislative competence over matters in **Entry 1 (Public Order)** and **Entry 2 (Police)** of the State List (Seventh Schedule); exclusive lawmaking power on these subjects was reserved for **Parliament** [24, 54].
    * **Planning & Master Plan Controls**: Matters relating to the implementation and modification of the Master Plan of Delhi were made subject to the approval of the **Governor** acting in his individual judgment, under general or special directions issued by the **President** [93].
  * **Schedule Amendments**: Made consequential modifications to the First Schedule (reclassifying Delhi under Part I States) and Fourth Schedule (allocating **3 seats** in the Council of States) [69, 76, 91].
* **Administration**: Central executive authority through the Governor (acting under Presidential direction) for reserved subjects, alongside the elected Legislative Assembly for other State List matters [24, 93].

* **Penalties**: **Not in record.** (The constitutional amendment contained no penal clauses; it was an enabling structural amendment [24, 93]).

* **Strongest Case For**: Replaces the inadequate advisory structure of the Delhi Administration Act, 1966 (the Metropolitan Council and Executive Council) with a democratic, directly elected legislative assembly, giving citizens an institutional voice and self-governance [76, 77].

### 1. WHAT IT IS
**The Bihar Reorganisation Bill, 2000** (enacted as the Bihar Reorganisation Act, 2000, Act No. 30 of 2000) is a constitutional reorganisation statute enacted to reconstitute the existing State of Bihar into two separate successor States: the residuary **State of Bihar** and the newly created State of **Jharkhand** [1, 2, 9]. The legislation transferred designated districts from the existing State of Bihar to Jharkhand to fulfill the democratic aspirations of the people of the region, while making incidental and supplemental provisions for legislative representation, apportionment of assets and liabilities, and inter-state administration [2, 9, 16].

---

### 2. OWNERSHIP & LEGAL STATUS
* **Ministry / Government Administration:** Handled at the Union level under constitutional powers governing the alteration of state boundaries (Articles 3 and 4 of the Constitution of India) [2, 9]. Specific administrative oversight for post-bifurcation development included a dedicated Unit established in the **Planning Commission** under the direct charge of the Deputy Chairman [16].
* **Parliamentary Passage & Stage:** Passed by the **Lok Sabha on 2 August 2000**, passed with amendments by the **Rajya Sabha on 11 August 2000**, with amendments agreed to by the Lok Sabha on **11 August 2000** [2].
* **Assent & Enactment:** Received the President's Assent on **25 August 2000** as **Act No. 30 of 2000** [2, 25].

---

### 3. DESIGN & KEY CLAUSES
* **Territorial Demarcation (Clauses 3 & 4):** Clause 3 carves out territories to form the State of Jharkhand, comprising Bokaro, Chatra, Deoghar, Dhanbad, Dumka, Garhwa, Giridih, Godda, Gumla, Hazaribagh, Kodarma, Lohardaga, Pakur, Palamau, Ranchi, Sahebganj, Singhbhum (East), and Singhbhum (West) districts [23]. Clause 4 defines the residuary State of Bihar as the territories remaining from the existing State [23, 24].
* **Constitutional Schedules (Clauses 5 & 7):** Amends the First Schedule to add Jharkhand as entry 28 [23, 40]. Amends the Fourth Schedule to reallocate Rajya Sabha seats: the existing Bihar allocation of 22 is reduced to **16 seats for Bihar**, and **6 seats are allocated to Jharkhand** [40].
* **Population Ratio (Clause 2(h)):** Fixed in the ratio of **645.30 : 218.44** between the residuary State of Bihar (approx. 645.30 lakh) and Jharkhand (approx. 218.44 lakh), pegged to the 1991 Census for asset and liability distribution [11, 16].
* **Apportionment of Assets & Liabilities (Clauses 40 & 41):** Financial revenues are apportioned based on orders by the President following Finance Commission recommendations under Article 280 [5, 37]. Clause 41 stipulates that successor States receive benefits and bear financial liabilities arising from decisions taken by the predecessor State, subject to equitable financial adjustments [37, 39].
* **Water Resources Board (Clauses 81 & 82):** Creates a Board for water resources management; any questions concerning the Board's jurisdiction are referred to the Central Government [7]. The Board is empowered under Clause 82 to make regulations with prior approval of the Central Government [7, 30].
* **Adaptation and Territorial Extent of Laws (Clauses 84 & 85):** Existing laws remain in force within former territorial boundaries until altered by a competent Legislature [18, 20]. Clause 85 permits the appropriate Government (Central Government for Union List matters; State Governments for other matters) up to **two years** from the appointed day to adapt or modify laws by order [8, 17].
* **Zonal Council:** Clause 83 amends Section 15(c) of the States Reorganisation Act, 1956 to substitute "Bihar" with "Bihar and Jharkhand" [18, 30].

* **Specific Penalties in the Bill:** **Not in record.** The Bill is a structural and reorganisation enactment governing state succession, legislative representation, and property apportionment; it does not contain a penal chapter or criminal penalties [1, 2, 4].

Following prior introduction of a 1998 Bill and examination by the Standing Committee on Finance and Select Committee of Rajya Sabha, the legislative framework was ultimately enacted as **The Prevention of Money-laundering Act, 2002** (Act No. 15 of 2003) [1, 2].

### 3. DESIGN

#### Offence and Key Clauses
* **Offence of Money-Laundering (Section 3):** Whosoever directly or indirectly attempts to indulge, knowingly assists, is a party to, or is actually involved in any process or activity connected with the proceeds of crime and projecting it as untainted property commits the offence of money-laundering [6, 7].
* **Obligations of Entities (Sections 12–15):** Banking companies, financial institutions, and intermediaries must maintain records of all prescribed transactions for **10 years** from the date of cessation of transactions and furnish information to the Director [4].
* **Attachment and Confiscation (Sections 5–8):** Provides provisional attachment of property involved in money-laundering, adjudication by an Adjudicating Authority upon a 30-day show-cause notice, and subsequent confiscation vesting all rights and title absolutely in the Central Government free from encumbrances [3, 8].
* **Search, Seizure, and Arrest (Sections 16–24):** Confers powers of survey, entry, search, seizure, and arrest upon the Director and authorized subordinate officers. Requires searches of females to be conducted exclusively by females [9, 10].
* **Burden of Proof & Presumptions (Sections 23–24):** In interconnected transactions, once one transaction is proven to be involved in money-laundering, remaining transactions are presumed connected unless disproved. Accused persons bear the burden of proving that alleged proceeds of crime are untainted [11].

#### Penalties
* **Primary Offence (Section 4):** Rigorous imprisonment for a minimum term of **3 years**, extendable up to **7 years**, alongside liability to a fine of up to **₹5 lakh** [6, 7].
* **Aggravated Offence (Narcotics / Paragraph 2 of Part A Schedule):** Where proceeds of crime relate to offences specified under paragraph 2 of Part A of the Schedule, the maximum term of imprisonment is extended up to **10 years** [7].
* **Non-compliance Penalties:** The Director is empowered to impose fines on banking companies, financial institutions, or intermediaries for failure to comply with transaction record-keeping and reporting mandates [4].

#### Administration & Enforcement
* **Administrative Hierarchy (Sections 48–49):** Administered by statutory authorities including the **Director**, Additional Director, Joint Director, Deputy Director, Assistant Director, and other officers appointed under Section 49 [5, 12].
* **Civil Court Powers (Section 50):** The Director holds civil court powers under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 regarding discovery, inspection, attendance enforcement, oath examination, and compelling document production [12, 13].
* **Adjudication & Appeals:** Independent **Adjudicating Authorities** (appointed under Section 6) adjudicate show-cause notices and confirm attachments, with statutory appeals lying to an **Appellate Tribunal** (established under Section 25) [5, 8].
* **Trial Mechanism:** Prosecutions and scheduled offences are tried before a designated **Special Court** (a Court of Session designated under Section 43) [14].

* **Strongest Case For:** Aligns India's domestic legal architecture with the UN Convention, UN General Assembly Resolutions, and FATF recommendations; creates robust multi-agency mechanisms to track cross-border illicit flows, confiscate illicit proceeds, and extradite offenders [1, 2, 15].
* **Strongest Case Against:** Stringent procedural shifts—including the reversal of the burden of proof to the accused under Section 24, wide search and seizure powers vested in executive authorities, and strict bail limits (which required the government to introduce specific relaxations for minors under 16, women, and the infirm) [11, 16].

### 3. DESIGN & KEY CLAUSES

* **Offence of Money Laundering (Chapter II, Section 3):** Any person who directly or indirectly attempts to indulge, knowingly assists, is knowingly a party, or is actually involved in any process or activity connected with proceeds of crime and projects it as untainted property is guilty of money laundering [6, 12].
* **Obligations of Entities (Sections 12–15):** Imposes obligations on banking companies, financial institutions, and intermediaries to maintain and furnish information on reportable transactions in the manner prescribed by the Central Government in consultation with the Reserve Bank of India [14].
* **Attachment & Adjudication (Chapters III & IV):** Authorises the appointment of an **Adjudicating Authority** (under Section 6) to adjudicate on attached properties, and designates **Special Courts** (Courts of Session under Section 43) for trial of scheduled offences and confiscation matters [6, 10, 15].
* **Search, Seizure & Enforcement (Chapter V, Sections 16–24):** Empowers the Director (or authorised officers) to carry out surveys, enter and search buildings, vessels, vehicles, or aircraft, break open locks, conduct personal searches, effect arrests, retain property/records, and reverse the burden of proof [14, 15].
* **Appeals:** Establishes an **Appellate Tribunal** under Section 25 [15].
* **Reciprocal International Assistance:** Includes reciprocal arrangements to facilitate the transfer of funds kept outside the country, mutual assistance, and extradition of accused persons from abroad [10, 11].

### 4. PENALTIES

* **Substantive Offence (Section 4):**
  * **Standard Offence:** Mandatory rigorous imprisonment of **not less than 3 years but which may extend to 7 years**, plus liability to a fine up to **₹5 lakh** [6, 12].
  * **Narcotics-Related Predicate Offence:** If proceeds of crime relate to offences specified under Paragraph 2 of Part A of the Schedule, the maximum term of imprisonment extends up to **10 years** [12].
* **Non-Compliance Penalties:** Empowers the Director to impose fines on banking companies, financial institutions, or intermediaries failing to adhere to reporting obligations under Section 12 [14]. Defaults regarding summons/directions are also subject to penal action [11].

---

### 5. TRADE-OFFS

* **Strongest Case For:** Aligns India's domestic legal architecture with the FATF's 40 recommendations and UN declarations; grants statutory powers to track criminal proceeds, attach illicit wealth, and seek international extradition and cross-border asset retrieval [7, 10, 11].
* **Strongest Case Against / Friction Points:** Stringent search and seizure powers vested in executive officers, reversal of the burden of proof (Section 24), and rigorous pre-trial bail conditions (which required explicit exceptions for women, minors under 16, and the sick or infirm) [11, 14, 15].

### 1. WHAT IT IS
The **Prevention of Money-Laundering Bill, 1999** (which culminated in the Prevention of Money-laundering Act, 2002 [Act No. 15 of 2003]) was introduced to prevent money laundering, confiscate property derived from or involved in money laundering, and implement international commitments [1, 2]. These included the United Nations Convention Against Illicit Traffic in Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances, the 1989 Basle Statement of Principles, the 40 recommendations of the Financial Action Task Force (FATF), and declarations adopted at the UN General Assembly Special Sessions in 1990 and 1998 [2, 3].

### 3. DESIGN

* **Offence Definition:** Anyone who directly or indirectly attempts to indulge, knowingly assists, is a party to, or is actually involved in any process or activity connected with the proceeds of crime and projects it as untainted property is guilty of money laundering [7, 8].
* **Obligations on Institutions:** Sections 12 to 15 require banking companies, financial institutions, and intermediaries to maintain and furnish transaction records, with procedures prescribed in consultation with the Reserve Bank of India [9].
* **Key Enforcement Powers (Chapter V):** Sections 16 to 24 empower authorities regarding surveys of premises, search and seizure operations, arrest, retention of property and records, and burden of proof [9, 10]. Under Section 17, the Director is empowered to authorise searches of premises, buildings, vessels, vehicles, or aircraft and seize records or property [10].

---

### 4. PENALTIES & PENAL PROVISIONS

* **Imprisonment and Fines:** The baseline offence is punishable with **rigorous imprisonment for 3 to 7 years** and a **fine extending up to ₹5 lakh** [7, 8].
* **Enhanced Penalty:** Where the proceeds of crime relate to offences specified under Paragraph 2 of Part A of the Schedule, the maximum term extends to **10 years** [8].
* **Regulatory Fines:** The Director has the power to impose fines on banking companies, financial institutions, or intermediaries failing to comply with record-keeping and reporting mandates under Section 12 [9].
* **Property Measures:** Provisions for the attachment, adjudication, and confiscation of proceeds of crime [8, 11].

---

### 5. ADMINISTRATION & AUTHORITIES

* **Director & Appointed Officers:** Appointed under Section 49 (including Assistant Directors), empowered with search, seizure, arrest, and imposition of fines on non-compliant institutions [5, 9, 10].
* **Adjudicating Authority:** Appointed under Section 6(1) to adjudicate matters relating to the attachment of property [5, 11].
* **Appellate Tribunal:** Established under Section 25 to hear appeals against regulatory and adjudicating orders [5].
* **Special Courts:** Designated Courts of Session under Section 43(1) for trying scheduled offences and related money laundering cases [7].

---

### 6. IMPLEMENTATION WATCH

* **Extradition and Cross-Border Assets:** Reciprocal arrangements and procedures for tracking and attaching overseas proceeds of crime or extraditing accused persons [12].
* **Bail Relaxations:** Specific statutory provisions permitting courts to grant bail to persons under 16 years of age, women, or those who are sick or infirm [12].
* **Subsequent Evolution:** Subsequent amendments (such as in 2005, 2009, and 2012) removed the ₹5 lakh fine ceiling, expanded definitions to include possession/concealment, introduced the concept of reporting entities, and transferred confiscation jurisdiction from the Adjudicating Authority to Special Courts [13, 14].
